title: Dating old hollow trees by applying a multistep tree-ring and radiocarbon procedure to trunk and exposed roots
author: Piovesan, Biondi, et al.

steps.title: Extract stem wood cores
steps.instruction: Using a standard 5 mm diameter increment borer, extract four wood cores from the trunk at breast height (≈1.3 m) and at additional heights between 0.5 m and 1.5 m.

steps.title: Crossdate stem ring series
steps.instruction: Measure ring widths of the four stem cores, average them, and cross‑date the resulting series against the regional master chronology using software such as Catras, reporting Student’s t and Gleichläufigkeit (GLK) statistics.

steps.title: Estimate missing inner rings
steps.instruction: Calculate the average width of the innermost 20–50 rings; use this average to estimate the number of missing rings between the pith and the first dated ring (e.g., 205–227 rings, giving an estimated pith date of 727–749 CE, age range 1 290–1 268 years). If the estimate is remarkable, decide whether large old exposed roots near the tap root can be sampled.

steps.title: Extract exposed root cores
steps.instruction: Using a modified increment borer, core the exposed vertical root system: first collect three external root cores (first campaign) and later two internal root cores (second campaign), targeting sections without bark and with minimal outer rings.

steps.title: Build floating root ring series
steps.instruction: Measure ring widths of all root cores, construct individual floating series (each 117–322 years long), and merge them into a composite floating average root series of 322 years.

steps.title: Select samples for radiocarbon dating
steps.instruction: From each root core, choose at least two wood samples spaced >20–30 years apart (total six samples: two per each of the three external root cores) for radiocarbon analysis.

steps.title: Prepare cellulose for AMS
steps.instruction: Chemically process each selected sample to extract pure cellulose using the “BABAB” method, then combust the cellulose to CO₂ in sealed quartz tubes, cryogenically purify the CO₂, and catalytically reduce it to graphite with H₂ as the reducing agent.

substeps.instruction: Combust cellulose in sealed quartz tubes to produce CO₂.
Catalytically reduce CO₂ to graphite using H₂.

steps.title: Measure 14C with AMS
steps.instruction: Load the graphite targets into the AMS system at CEDAD (3 MV Tandetron accelerator) and measure the ¹⁴C content of each sample.

steps.title: Calibrate dates and wiggle match
steps.instruction: Calibrate the conventional radiocarbon ages of the six samples in OxCal using Bayesian statistical tools; perform wiggle‑matching of each calibrated pair (Root1, Root2, Root3) against the floating root series.

substeps.instruction: Enter radiocarbon ages into OxCal and run Bayesian calibration.
Independently calibrate each pair of samples from the same root.
Apply wiggle‑matching using the floating root series as the reference.

steps.title: Synchronize root and stem series
steps.instruction: Search the wiggle‑matched radiocarbon window for a significant synchronization between a root series (e.g., R2) and the stem series; evaluate statistical support (t‑value = 3.45, GLK = 63.0 %, significant at 99 %) and assign the corresponding calendar year (e.g., 878 CE) to the oldest radiocarbon‑dated root sample.

steps.title: Determine final tree age
steps.instruction: Combine the cross‑dated stem ring series with the radiocarbon‑dated, synchronized root series to obtain a composite chronology, yielding a minimum tree age of 1 229 years for the hollow tree.

description: This multistep tree-ring and radiocarbon dating procedure for age determination of old hollow trees was applied to a Pinus heldreichii named Italus, located in Pollino National Park, southern Italy [4].1)Four wood cores 5-mm in diameter were extracted from the stem of Italus at different height level (0.5–1.5 m) using an increment borer (Fig. 1). A crossdated tree-ring series (Fig. 2) revealed a remarkable age for the species [4,12] and for the subgenus Diploxylon ([13], see also Oldlist http://www.rmtrr.org/oldlist.htm).Fig. 1The millennium-old pine tree named Italus. Wood cores were extracted at breast height (∼1.3 m; red dot; stem) and from the exposed vertical root system using a modified increment borer (also shown, red square and lower inset box).Fig. 1Fig. 2Comparison of crossdated tree-ring series for Italus - developed by averaging 4 stem cores - with the Pollino master chronology. Student’s t and Gleichläufigkeit (GLK) statistics, calculated by software Catras [7] are shown in the box. GLK measures the percentage of common signs of year-to-year growth change between two series.Fig. 22)Age estimation based on the average width of the innermost 20–50 rings suggested 205–227 rings between the missing pith and the first dated ring. The estimated pith date was 727–749 CE (age range 1290–1268 years), making Italus a likely candidate for one of the most longeve trees in Europe.3)Wood cores were extracted from the exposed root system in two successive periods. During a first campaign, three cores located in the external part of the old exposed root system were sampled (Fig. 3, red box) and used for constructing a floating tree-ring series and for radiocarbon analyses.
